requirements.requirement: Create an SSH certificate authority on node1
requirements.summary: An ed25519 CA keypair was generated at /etc/ssh/ca/ssh_ca with restrictive private-key permissions (600) and a readable public key (644), fingerprint SHA256:UtvoUCfbeeoEV4jqF5WBxEMKLx6gjR7RW1qcYH3gBYM.

requirements.requirement: Host presents a certificate signed by the CA
requirements.summary: The node's existing ed25519 host public key was signed by the CA into /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key-cert.pub with principals node1, 10.100.247.10, localhost, 10-year validity, and the certificate's Signing CA fingerprint matches the CA generated in the prior step.

requirements.requirement: sshd is configured to actually offer the certificate to clients
requirements.summary: A HostCertificate drop-in was added and validated (sshd -t, sshd -T showing hostcertificate directive). An initial SELinux mislabel (tmp_t) on the cert file silently prevented sshd from loading it (confirmed via journalctl 'Could not load host certificate'); this was diagnosed and fixed with chcon/semanage fcontext to sshd_key_t, after which a clean sshd restart showed no load errors and a live client handshake showed the server presenting the ssh-ed25519-cert-v01 certificate.

requirements.requirement: A client trusting only the CA (no pinned host key) connects successfully; trust flows from the CA, not from an incidentally pinned key
requirements.summary: A test client with known_hosts containing only '@cert-authority * <ca pubkey>' connected successfully and the client explicitly logged 'Host is known and matches the ED25519-CERT host certificate' before authenticating and running a command. A control run with an empty known_hosts file failed with 'No matching CA found' / 'Host key verification failed', confirming the success case depended on CA trust rather than any pinned key.

overall_summary: The executor created an ed25519 SSH CA on node1, signed the host's ed25519 key into a certificate, configured sshd to serve it, root-caused and fixed a real SELinux mislabeling defect that was silently blocking certificate loading, and directly demonstrated (via live SSH client transcripts) that a client trusting only the CA's public key connects and validates the host via the certificate — with a matching negative control proving the trust is CA-derived. The mandatory reboot protocol was also completed with a clearly changed boot_id (cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots) and re-verified post-reboot service and CA-trust state, and all test artifacts were cleaned up.
limitations: Only one client trust round-trip was captured per state (pre-reboot and post-reboot); no evidence of testing a hostname-based principal beyond the IP-based check, though 'node1' and 'localhost' principals were included in the certificate.

Evidence is drawn from ssh -v/-vvv debug output and journalctl from within the executor's own session rather than a fully independent third-party client, though this is standard and sufficient for this kind of verification.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing executor commands map clearly to the task: CA creation, host-cert signing, sshd config drop-in, the SELinux relabel/fcontext fix (a necessary correction for a real defect the executor caused/discovered), and sshd restarts to load the fixed config. Temporary test artifacts (test client keys, temporary known_hosts files, authorized_keys entries used only to validate host-side trust) were added and then removed in the same session (cmd-4982dca4678d4ea8, cmd-a9566b6077944161) and again after the post-reboot re-verification (cmd-373a79bf916b4faa). The mandatory node-restart protocol (systemctl reboot) was executed and is itself a required action, not an unnecessary mutation. No abandoned files, no failed services, and package-health/listening-socket baselines are unchanged in substance (only PID/boot-id churn from the reboot) per the lifecycle comparison.
